blocks.title: Voice
blocks.md: An **unreliable narrator** gives a view that the reader learns to doubt (through bias, self-deception, or lack of knowledge). **Free indirect speech** blends narrator and character voice: ‘He would never forgive them. Never.’ without ‘he thought’. **Stream of consciousness** presents thoughts as they flow. A **frame narrative** places one story inside another.

blocks.title: Time and structure
blocks.md: **Flashback** moves back in time, **foreshadowing** hints at future events, **chronology** can be linear or fragmented. **Pace** is controlled by summary (fast) and scene (slow). **Irony** arises when meaning differs from appearance: **verbal** (saying the opposite), **situational** (outcome contrary to expectation), **dramatic** (reader knows more than character).

blocks.caption: Narrative techniques and their effects.
blocks.alt: A table of four narrative techniques and their effects.

blocks.title: Commenting on technique
blocks.md: Name the technique, quote briefly, explain **how the reader’s understanding is shaped**, and link to theme. Ask: Why this narrator? Why this order? What is withheld, and why?

blocks.title: Avoid
blocks.md:
- Calling every first-person narrator unreliable: look for evidence of doubt.
- Identifying a device without discussing its effect.
- Confusing the author’s views with the narrator’s.

blocks.title: Example 1 — Unreliable narration
blocks.statement: Original extract: ‘I have always been the fairest man in this district. If the tenants whisper that I raised the rent twice this year, it is because they cannot count. Mr Fon, who I will not name again, has the nerve to say that I am hard.’ Comment on the narrator.
steps: Self-praise at the start is a claim the reader must test.
He blames tenants for ‘not counting’ and avoids denying the rent rises.
The reader infers that he is defensive, self-deceiving and probably unfair: an unreliable narrator.
blocks.answer: He undermines himself; the reader doubts his account.

blocks.title: Example 2 — Foreshadowing
blocks.statement: Original sentence: ‘That morning the cock crowed three times before anyone moved, and Mama said nothing about the cracked mirror.’ What might the sentence foreshadow?
steps: Unusual signs (the cock, the cracked mirror) are the kind of detail linked to bad omens.
Mama’s silence suggests worry.
The reader expects misfortune.

blocks.title: Why compare?
blocks.md: Comparison shows how **different poets treat a similar theme** through **form, imagery, sound, tone and speaker**. You look for **similarities** and **differences** and explain why they matter. A comparison is not two separate commentaries: keep both poems in view in every paragraph (the **integrated** method).

blocks.title: Structure
blocks.md: Introduction: name the shared theme and state the main contrast. Then take **points** (for example attitude to the city, imagery, form, ending) and compare both poems within each. Use connectives: *similarly, in contrast, whereas, both, by comparison, however*. End with a judgement about the poems’ effects.

blocks.caption: Structure of a poetry comparison.
blocks.alt: Four boxes: theme and contrast, points, both poems in each paragraph and a judgement.

blocks.title: What to compare
blocks.md: **Speaker and situation**; **tone** and any shift; **imagery** (type and effect); **form** (stanza, rhyme, rhythm, line length); **sound**; **ending**; **message or theme**. Support every comparison with brief quotation.

blocks.title: Common faults
blocks.md:
- Writing all about poem A, then all about poem B with no links.
- Treating features as equal when one matters more.
- Ignoring form and sound.
- Overlong quotations.

blocks.title: Example 1 — Spot similarities and differences
blocks.statement: Original poems on a town. Poem A: ‘The town is a drum that never rests, / its lorries beating on my chest.’ Poem B: ‘Between the stalls the evening glows, / and every stranger greets and goes.’ Compare their view of town life.
steps: Both use sound and image to present the town.
A: harsh, noisy, oppressive metaphor (drum, beating on my chest).
B: warm, friendly mood (glows, greets).
Similar couplet form but contrasting attitudes: stress versus comfort.
blocks.answer: Both are couplets about the town but A is oppressive and B is warm.

blocks.title: Example 2 — Write a comparative sentence
blocks.statement: Write one comparative sentence linking the two poems.
steps: Use a connective and refer to both poems with quotations.
‘Whereas poem A presents the town as an oppressive ‘drum’, poem B softens it with the warm image of an ‘evening glows’, showing different attitudes to the same setting.’
blocks.answer: A sentence with connective and two quotations.

blocks.title: Speaker and addressee
blocks.md: The **speaker** (persona) of a poem is not always the poet. A **dramatic monologue** is a poem in which a character speaks to a silent listener and reveals more than they intend, so the reader reads between the lines. Ask: who is speaking, to whom, in what situation, and what does the speaker fail to notice?

blocks.title: The sonnet
blocks.md: A **sonnet** has fourteen lines, usually with a rhyme scheme and a **volta** (turn) where the argument or mood shifts. The **Shakespearean** sonnet has three quatrains and a final couplet (ABAB CDCD EFEF GG); the **Petrarchan** has an octave and a sestet. The compact form pushes the poet to concentrate an idea, and the turn changes direction.

blocks.caption: Two common sonnet structures.
blocks.alt: A table with the Shakespearean and Petrarchan sonnet structures.

blocks.title: Analysing voice and form
blocks.md: Identify the speaker, tone and any **irony** between what is said and what is shown. Note the form, rhyme and where the turn occurs, and explain how the structure supports the meaning, for example by delaying the main idea until the couplet. Use short quotations.

blocks.title: Avoid
blocks.md:
- Assuming that ‘I’ in a poem is the poet.
- Saying that a sonnet is about love by definition: sonnets treat many themes.
- Naming the volta without explaining what changes.

blocks.title: Example 1 — Dramatic monologue
blocks.statement: Original lines: ‘Of course I am not angry. I merely mention that the fence you built stands one foot on my land; but I am not angry. Please have more tea.’ Comment on the speaker.
steps: The speaker denies anger while describing a grievance.
‘I merely mention’ and ‘Please have more tea’ show forced politeness.
The reader sees irritation beneath the calm: ironic self-revelation.
blocks.answer: Politeness masks anger; the speaker reveals more than intended.

blocks.title: Example 2 — The turn
blocks.statement: Original sonnet closing lines: ‘For years I called this valley mine alone— / yet now the river sings to every home.’ What does the turn do?
steps: The ‘yet’ marks the volta.
It moves from possession (‘mine alone’) to sharing (‘every home’).
The final couplet gives a gentle resolution.
blocks.answer: It shifts from private ownership to shared belonging.

blocks.title: What is context?
blocks.md: **Context** is the setting in which a text is written and read: historical events, social attitudes, culture, literary tradition, the author’s life and the audience. Context can **illuminate** a text, but the essay must stay about the text’s words. Distinguish the **context of writing** from the **context of reception** (how readers today respond).

blocks.title: Using context well
blocks.md: Make context **relevant** and **brief**: one or two sentences linked to a specific detail in the text. Show how the context affects meaning (for example, a text written under strict social rules may use indirect speech). Avoid biographical guesses and unverified claims.

items.text: Reader: allow more than one reading
Judgement: which reading is most convincing

blocks.caption: Using context and the reader in an essay.
blocks.alt: Four boxes: text, context, reader and judgement.

blocks.title: The reader
blocks.md: Readers bring their own experience, so interpretations differ. A good essay allows for **more than one reading**, supports each with evidence and decides which is most convincing. Awareness of audience and purpose (to entertain, to persuade, to criticise) also helps.

blocks.title: Pitfalls
blocks.md:
- Dropping historical facts without linking them to the text.
- Making unverified claims about an author’s life.
- Treating context as the whole answer.
- Forgetting that readers today may respond differently.

blocks.title: Example 1 — Relevant context
blocks.statement: Original text: a story from an imaginary society where young people must ask elders’ permission to speak. A character says, ‘If it is allowed, I would like to be silent.’ How might context help?
steps: Knowing that speaking requires permission explains the polite phrasing.
It shows that silence may be a protest or a safe choice.
Context illuminates tone but the reading must rest on the words.
blocks.answer: The social rule explains the indirect speech and gives the line irony.

blocks.title: Example 2 — Two readings
blocks.statement: Original sentence: ‘The new school stood tall, and the old tree fell for it.’ Give two readings.
steps: Reading 1: progress replaces nature; the tree is a sacrifice.
Reading 2: the tree ‘fell for’ the school like someone falling in love: humour and affection for the community’s change.
Both rest on wordplay: ‘fell for it’.
blocks.answer: Progress versus loss, or playful affection through wordplay.

exercises.prompt: Original sentence: ‘The doctor assured everyone that the bridge was perfectly safe, and then went home by the long road.’ Explain the irony.
exercises.model: The doctor’s words claim safety, but his own choice to avoid the bridge shows he does not trust it. This is verbal and situational irony: what he says contradicts what he does. It invites the reader to distrust the reassurance.
exercises.explanation: The doctor’s words claim safety, but his own choice to avoid the bridge shows he does not trust it. This is verbal and situational irony: what he says contradicts what he does. It invites the reader to distrust the reassurance.

exercises.source: Original exercise written for CastBridge, in the style of the curriculum
exercises.prompt: Original extract: ‘My brother says I am stubborn. He forgets who paid for his schooling, who found him the job, who sat up through his fever. Stubborn! I have simply never been wrong.’ Write a paragraph on how the writer presents the narrator.
exercises.model: The narrator seems proud and self-justifying. The list of favours reveals resentment, while the exclamation ‘Stubborn!’ shows irritation. The final claim ‘never been wrong’ is absolute and comic, making him unreliable and slightly blind to his own faults. The rhythm of repeated ‘who’ builds accusation.
exercises.rubric: Tone identified (1); repetition/list (1); absolute claim (1); effect of unreliability (1).

exercises.source: Original exercise written for CastBridge, in the style of the curriculum
exercises.prompt: Original: Poem A ‘The sea is a door that opens in the night’; Poem B ‘The sea is a wall, grey and shut’. Write a comparative paragraph on the sea.
exercises.model: Both poems use a metaphor for the sea, but they differ in what it suggests. In A the sea is a ‘door’ that ‘opens’, which suggests possibility and mystery; in B it is a ‘wall, grey and shut’, which suggests limits and despair. Whereas A’s verb is active and hopeful, B’s adjectives are static and cold.
exercises.rubric: Both poems considered (1); contrasting readings (2); quotations (1).
exercises.explanation: Both poems use a metaphor for the sea, but they differ in what it suggests. In A the sea is a ‘door’ that ‘opens’, which suggests possibility and mystery; in B it is a ‘wall, grey and shut’, which suggests limits and despair. Whereas A’s verb is active and hopeful, B’s adjectives are static and cold.

exercises.source: Original exercise written for CastBridge, in the style of the curriculum
exercises.prompt: Original pair. Poem X (regular rhyme): ‘We plant the maize, we pray for rain, / we wait, we hope, we plant again.’ Poem Y (free verse): ‘The field is cracked. / I stand. / Nobody speaks.’ Compare how each poem presents hardship.
exercises.model: Both present hardship in farming, but X uses regular rhyme and repetition (‘we plant’) to show persistent, almost ritual endurance and hope; its pattern suggests an unbroken cycle. Y uses short free-verse lines and silence to show stark despair: the cracked field and the lack of speech suggest defeat. X is resilient, Y is bleak, and the forms enhance each mood.
exercises.rubric: Similarity (1); contrast in tone (1); form comparison (1); supported by quotation (1).
exercises.explanation: Both present hardship in farming, but X uses regular rhyme and repetition (‘we plant’) to show persistent, almost ritual endurance and hope; its pattern suggests an unbroken cycle. exercises.model: The denial of jealousy is contradicted by the careful comparison of roofs, so the speaker reveals envy and insecurity. The humour comes from the gap between what is said and what is shown.

exercises.source: Original exercise written for CastBridge, in the style of the curriculum
exercises.prompt: Original sonnet couplet-ending: ‘And so the clock keeps time, but I keep none; / the evening comes, and finds me almost done.’ Discuss how the final couplet might work as a conclusion.
exercises.model: The couplet’s rhyme (none/done) gives closure and a sense of resignation. The clock imagery contrasts mechanical time with the speaker’s lack of control, so the ending expresses acceptance and a note of weariness. It resolves the poem’s tension quietly.
exercises.rubric: Rhyme and closure (1); imagery (1); tone (1); effect (1).
exercises.explanation: The couplet’s rhyme (none/done) gives closure and a sense of resignation. The clock imagery contrasts mechanical time with the speaker’s lack of control, so the ending expresses acceptance and a note of weariness. It resolves the poem’s tension quietly.

exercises.source: Original exercise written for CastBridge, in the style of the curriculum
exercises.prompt: Original sentence from a story: ‘The telegram arrived on market day, and no one dared open it before the drums began.’ Write a short paragraph using context sensibly to comment on the sentence.
exercises.model: The telegram suggests a time when news came slowly and often meant trouble, and the delay until the drums began shows a community custom of gathering before receiving serious news. The phrase ‘no one dared’ creates tension and suggests the weight of the unknown. Context helps explain the ritual but the effect comes from the writer’s choice of words.
exercises.rubric: Context linked to detail (1); language (1); effect (1); balance (1).
exercises.explanation: The telegram suggests a time when news came slowly and often meant trouble, and the delay until the drums began shows a community custom of gathering before receiving serious news. The phrase ‘no one dared’ creates tension and suggests the weight of the unknown. Context helps explain the ritual but the effect comes from the writer’s choice of words.
